Telugu New Year; homes are decorated and Ugadi pachadi is prepared.

Ganesh festival with clay idols and community pandals.
Navratri celebrations; major at Kanaka Durga Temple, Vijayawada.
Festival of lights celebrated statewide.
Night-long Shiva worship; biggest at Srisailam Mallikarjuna.

The Vaikuntha Dwaram opens at Tirumala; huge devotee turnout.
Navratri celebrations on Indrakeeladri with the goddess in nine avatars.

Tribal communities celebrate the harvest with Dhimsa dance and local rituals.

Buddha Purnima celebrations at the Amaravati stupa and Dhyana Buddha statue.

Goa's famous pre-Lent street carnival; Panaji hosts the main float parade led by King Momo (in 2026 the Panaji grand parade ran on Feb 14, from New Patto Bridge to Campal Ground). Colourful floats, music bands and dance troupes across the city.

Goa's spring harvest festival with vibrant folk dances, traditional music and colourful float parades; Panaji hosts one of the state's biggest parades (in 2026 the Panaji parade was on March 7, part of a March 5-18 statewide celebration across 19 centres).
Annual parish feast of Fontainhas' Chapel of St. Sebastian, celebrated on 20 January with community festivities around the chapel.

festival_name: Feast of Our Lady of Livrament
description: Mid-November street fair outside the Chapel of St. Sebastian in Fontainhas, celebrating the Feast of Our Lady of Livrament.
Monsoon festival honouring St. John the Baptist, celebrated across Goa (including Panaji) on June 24 with the tradition of young men jumping into wells and rivers; linked to the onset of the monsoon.

Goa's pre-Lent street carnival; Margao's float parade runs from Holy Spirit Church to the Margao Municipal Council Square, one of the state's biggest south-Goa celebrations. In the 2026 edition the Margao parade fell on 15 February.

festival_name: Feast of Our Lady of Grace Church
description: Annual feast of Margao's modern landmark church (built 1970), celebrated on the first Sunday of February with masses, processions and community feasts.
Goa's traditional spring harvest festival with colourful float parades, folk dance and music; Margao hosts one of the state-level Shigmo parades (5-18 March in 2026).

festival_name: Feast of the Holy Spirit Church
description: Annual parish feast of Margao's landmark 17th-century church, celebrated around Pentecost (reported as Sunday 15 May in recent coverage) with concelebrated feast mass and parish celebrations.
Catholic monsoon festival (24 June) celebrated across Salcete/Margao with the tradition of jumping into wells and rivers; neighbourhood processions and feasting.
Major Hindu festival celebrated widely across Goa; Margao sees large public pandals, immersion processions and household celebrations.

Vasco's signature week-long festival, held from the 6th day of the Hindu month of Shravan. Commemorates the 1898/1899 epidemic believed to have been ended by Lord Damodar's blessings; features 24-hour non-stop bhajans, a tableau procession, nightly cultural programmes and a large mela fair along Swatantra Path, with the Shri Damodar Temple in Vaddem as the main venue.
Patronal feast of Vasco's St Andrew's Church on 30 November, celebrated with novenas, a feast mass and processions through the town, drawing the city's Catholic community.
Goa's pre-Lent street carnival, celebrated across the state including Vasco, with float parades, music, dance and the King Momo procession in the days before Ash Wednesday.
Goa's spring folk festival of colours, celebrated with street parades of floats, traditional folk dances and gulal, observed in towns across Goa including Vasco.

The Catholic monsoon festival honouring St John the Baptist, celebrated across Goa with young men jumping into wells and streams, feni, and festive processions; observed in Vasco's Catholic neighbourhoods.

Annual feast of Our Lady of Miracles (Milagr Saibinnichem Fest) at St. Jerome Church, held on the 15th day after Easter, so it falls in April or May depending on the year. Thousands of Catholic and Hindu devotees throng the church for the novenas and feast day.

Annual week-long zatra (temple fair) at Shri Dev Bodgeshwar Sansthan, held in January, with over a hundred stalls selling clothes, footwear, utensils, food and games plus amusement rides like the giant wheel; evenings are very crowded. Sundays are observed as the deity's special day with heavy footfall.

Goa's state spring festival (Shigmotsav) celebrated in the Phalguna month; colourful float parades with folk dance, music and mythological tableaux are held across 19 centres in the state, with the Mapusa parade taking place in early March (Mapusa was a parade centre on March 8 in 2026).
Goa's biggest Hindu spring festival, celebrated with vibrant float parades, folk dances and gulal; Ponda hosts one of the major Shigmo parades, drawing crowds from across the state.
The annual chariot festival of Shri Manguesh Temple at Mangeshi, held in the Hindu month of Magha, with the deity's palanquin procession and thousands of devotees.
The annual zatra of Shri Navdurga Temple, Madkai, held during Kartika from Vidya Chaturthi to Dashami; Navratri is also celebrated here with great pomp.

Goa's exuberant monsoon mud festival at Shri Devki Krishna Temple, Marcel, on Ashadha Dwadashi — devotees play in rain-soaked slush reenacting Lord Krishna's childhood games (held 24–26 Jul in 2026, 5–7 Jul in 2025).
The annual jatra of Shri Vijayadurga Temple at Keri, famed for the lighting of its majestic deepastambha and the temple's rare Kaavi-art murals.
Goa's pre-Lent street carnival with parades, floats, music and dancing across North Goa, including the Baga-Calangute belt.
Goa's spring harvest festival with folk dances and colourful parades celebrated across the state, including Bardez taluka.

festival_name: Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe (Khelleam Fest), St. Alex Church
description: The main annual feast of Calangute's St. Alex parish, celebrated around mid-December with masses, processions and village festivities.

festival_name: Christmas and New Year beach celebrations
description: Peak-season beach parties, live music and fireworks along Calangute and Baga beaches through the Christmas-New Year week.
Goa's pre-Lent street carnival with float parades, music and dancing across the state, including the North Goa belt around Anjuna; the 2026 edition ran Feb 13-17 per the Goa tourism department.
Goa's spring harvest festival with folk dances and colourful float parades across 19 centres in the state, including Bardez taluka; the 2026 edition ran Mar 5-18 per the Goa tourism department.

Catholic feast of St. John the Baptist on Jun 24, marked by well-jumping, kopel flower crowns, feni and decorated boat parades (sangodd); boats arrive from Anjuna for the famous Siolim boat parade on the Chapora river.
Annual multi-day psytrance festival at HillTop, Vagator, usually in February (2024 edition Feb 25-27; listed as 'February annually'), with international and local trance acts across multiple stages.
Peak-season marathon trance parties at HillTop and Anjuna's beach shacks through the Christmas-New Year week, the busiest party fortnight of the Goan season.

festival_name: Feast of St. Michael the Archangel
description: Annual parish feast of St. Michael's Church, Anjuna, with masses, processions and village festivities; sources conflict on the exact date (Sept 29 vs first Sunday of October), so shown as Sep-Oct.
Goa's big pre-Lent street festival with parades, floats, music and dancing across the state; Canacona hosts its own celebrations and Palolem's beach crowd joins the party season.
Goa's spring festival of colour and folk dance; the Shri Mallikarjun Temple at Sristhal celebrates Shigmotsav, drawing devotees from across Canacona.
The monsoon Catholic festival where revellers jump into wells and streams to honour St. John the Baptist — celebrated in villages around Canacona with music, feni and new-rain feasts.
One of Goa's most important Hindu festivals; Canacona's homes and temples install Ganesh idols with days of prayers, music and festive food.

festival_name: Christmas and New Year's Eve beach parties
description: Palolem's peak party fortnight — Silent Noise, Leopard Valley and the beach shacks run headline nights; the beach fills with bonfires, live music and midnight celebrations.
Not a festival but a seasonal wildlife event: Olive Ridley turtles nest on Galgibaga, Agonda and nearby beaches; forest-department hatcheries guard nests and release hatchlings.
Old Goa's biggest annual religious festival, centered on the Basilica of Bom Jesus. Novena Masses run Nov 23-Dec 2, with the main feast on Dec 3.

festival_name: Exposition of the Sacred Relics of St Francis Xavier
description: Held once a decade at the Basilica of Bom Jesus; the saint's relics are brought down for public veneration over ~45 days, drawing millions of pilgrims.
approx_month: Once every ~10 years, typically November-January; most recent: November 2024 - January 2025

description: Midnight Mass and celebrations at Se Cathedral and the Old Goa churches; the heritage churches are lit and decorated.
Float parade and festivities across Goa including Old Goa; Portuguese-era tradition with King Momo presiding.
Goa's spring folk festival with street parades, gulal, floats and folk dances in villages across the state, including areas around Old Goa.
Flag festival of Divar Island (Piedade village, ~3 km from Old Goa) — mock flag battles with toy weapons, a traditional harvest-season celebration.

Colva's biggest feast: the second Monday of October marks the ceremonial opening of the Menino Jesus (Infant Jesus) shrine at Our Lady of Mercy Church, drawing thousands of pilgrims for early-morning Mass, a procession of the 17th-century statue and fireworks.

festival_name: Sao Joao (Feast of St. John the Baptist, Benaulim)
description: Feast of St. John the Baptist at the church on Monte Benaulim (June 24). After Mass, the Goa-wide Sao Joao tradition sees young men in leafy crowns jumping into wells and streams, singing 'Viva San Joao'.

Gujarat's flagship kite festival held on the Sabarmati Riverfront around Uttarayan (14 January): the sky fills with kites as international flyers join lakhs of locals on rooftops; kite markets across the old city sell for weeks beforehand.
Week-long cultural festival (25-31 December) at the Kankaria Lakefront: food stalls, folk performances, adventure activities and fireworks marking the new year at the lake.
Classical dance festival held in the third week of January against the illuminated Sun Temple at Modhera (~100 km from Ahmedabad), organised by Gujarat Tourism.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya-raas across Ahmedabad's grounds and clubs - the city's biggest celebration, with all-night dancing, traditional chaniya choli and festive food.
The 150+ year-old Jagannath Rath Yatra from the Jamalpur temple on Ashadhi Bij - Ahmedabad's largest religious procession with decorated chariots, elephants and lakhs of devotees.

Surat's own firecracker festival celebrated the day after Dussehra, when the city famously bursts crackers through the night; a uniquely Surati tradition tied to the diamond and textile merchant community.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya raas; Surat hosts some of Gujarat's biggest garba venues and the whole city dances through the nights.
Festival of lights celebrated across Surat with fireworks, sweets (notably Surati ghari) and new clothes; markets in the old city stay packed late.
The kite festival on Makar Sankranti; Surat's skies fill with kites and rooftops host kite-flying parties with undhiyu and jalebi.

Vadodara is widely called the garba capital of the world, and Navratri's nine nights are the city's defining festival. The United Way of Baroda Garba Mahotsav (held 2026 at M M Patel Farm, Atladara, 9 PM onwards) draws 40,000+ participants nightly and set the 2022 world record for the most garba dancers at a single venue; funds raised support community welfare. Dozens of other grounds - Fine Arts (MSU students, traditional instruments), Vadodara Navratri Festival, Karelibaug Sports Garba and more - draw over three lakh players city-wide, insured for Rs 30.18 crore in 2024. Register online well in advance; late-night street food (pani puri, aloo tikki, bhel) completes the night.

Vadodara celebrates Makar Sankranti (January 14) as Uttarayan, when the sky fills with kites from dawn to night. Gujarat Tourism's International Kite Festival circuit includes Vadodara - in 2026 it was hosted at Navlakhi Ground with kite flyers from 50+ countries, giant inflatable kites, night kite flying (tukkals), cultural performances and street food like undhiyu and jalebi-fafda. Locals shout 'Kai Po Che!' during rooftop kite battles across the city.

The MG Vadodara International Marathon (Vadodara Marathon) is one of India's largest city marathons - AIMS and AFI certified, with over 1,00,000 registrations in recent editions across full, half, quarter, divyang, corporate and NGO pledge runs. Held each January (11th edition on January 7, 2025) and flagged off from Navlakhi Polo Ground; each edition champions a social cause (Fit India, organ donation).

Diwali, the festival of lights, is one of Vadodara's biggest celebrations: markets in Mandvi, Raopura and Alkapuri overflow with diyas, rangoli and sweets; homes light diyas on Lakshmi Puja; and the Laxmi Vilas Palace area glows with festive lighting. Sursagar's surroundings and the old-city bazaars are the best evening walks of the season.

Saurashtra's biggest annual fair, held on the Race Course Ground during the Krishna Janmashtami (Satam-Aathma) period. The 2026 edition ran 2-6 September as 'Virasatthi Vikas Lok Mela 2026' with daily cultural programmes in the late afternoon and evening.
The nine-night festival of the Goddess celebrated with garba and dandiya-raas dancing at venues across Rajkot; one of Gujarat's most famous festivals and a major draw for visitors.
The Diwali festival of lights is celebrated across the city, with the Annakut (Govardhan Puja) mountain-of-food offering at the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir as a major devotional attraction.
Gujarat's kite festival on Makar Sankranti; the skies over Rajkot fill with kites and rooftops host traditional kite-flying with undhiyu and jalebi.
The spring festival of colours celebrated in Rajkot with gulal and traditional festivities.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya raas; Gandhinagar's sector community grounds host garba venues and the whole city dances through the nights.
Festival of lights celebrated across the city; Akshardham and the sector gardens are lit up and markets stay packed late.
The kite festival on Makar Sankranti; terraces across Gandhinagar fill with kite flyers from dawn.
Three-day classical dance festival held in the third week of January against the backdrop of the Sun Temple at Modhera, about 90 km from Gandhinagar.

The annual Shatrunjay Teerth Yatra is held on Kartik Purnima (the full-moon day of the Kartik month), when thousands of Jains gather at the base of Shatrunjaya Hill near Palitana for the sacred hill circumambulation; devotees believe a yatra on this day is a once-in-a-lifetime event.

The famous annual fair at Nishkalank Mahadev Temple on Koliyak beach, held in the month of Shravan. The fair is traditionally inaugurated with a flag hoisted by descendants of Bhavnagar's royal family, and the flag reportedly stands through the tides all year.

Jamnagar Municipal Corporation-organised fair that runs from Janmashtami Day till the end of the Shravan month, drawing 4-5 lakh visitors with shopping stalls, food, rides, cultural shows and public-awareness booths.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya raas across the city; Jamnagar is noted for the traditional Indhoni Raas Garba, where women dance with a flaming indhoni (pot-holder) balanced on their heads.
Birth anniversary of Lord Krishna celebrated on a grand scale in Jamnagar, with fairs held at Jamnagar and nearby Dwarka and special festivities at Krishna temples across the city.

A five-day fair at the Bhavnath Mahadev Temple culminating on Maha Shivratri night, when Naga sadhus process with elephants, drums and conch shells and take a holy bath in the Mrigi Kund. One of Gujarat's greatest religious gatherings.
A five-day circumambulation of the Girnar hills (about 36 km) held around Kartik Purnima, starting from the Bhavnath temple. Thousands of pilgrims, sadhus and travellers walk the parikrama path.
A large fair held at the sacred Damodar Kund lake on Bhadrapada Amavasya (no-moon day), drawing devotees for holy dips and religious rituals at the Girnar foothills.
Krishna's birthday is celebrated at Sudama Temple and Dwarka-side shrines, and the Chowpati ground at Chowpatty Beach hosts Porbandar's annual Janmashtami fair.
The nine-night festival is celebrated across the city; the Huzoor Palace grounds are opened to the public during Navratri for the traditional nazar (viewing) of the royal family.

A five-day fair held at Madhavpur Ghed (~60 km, Porbandar district) starting on Ram Navami, commemorating the wedding of Krishna and Rukmini at the Madhavrai Temple, with folk performances from Gujarat and North-Eastern states under the Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat initiative.
2 October marks Mahatma Gandhi's birth anniversary with special ceremonies at Kirti Mandir, his birthplace memorial.

Three-day classical dance festival organized by Gujarat Tourism on the temple premises during the third week of January, following Uttarayan. Dancers from across India perform against the illuminated 11th-century Sun Temple backdrop.
The biggest fair at the Ambaji Shakti Peeth on the full moon of Bhadrapada; millions of devotees, many walking as foot pilgrims, visit the shrine and Gabbar Hill during the festive period.

festival_name: Taranga Kartik and Chaitra Purnima Melas
description: The two main annual full-moon pilgrimages at the Taranga Jain temples, drawing large Jain congregations to the 12th-century Ajitnath temple complex.
Traditional annual fairs at the Bahucharaji Mata temple on the full moons of Chaitra and Ashadh, attracting devotees from across North Gujarat.

Unique to Bharuch — celebrated nowhere else in India. A 5.5-foot idol of Meghraj (Lord Indra) is sculpted from Narmada river soil and worshipped for 25 days in the month of Shravan; a fair (mela) is organised during the last four days of the festival.
Every Saturday in the month of Shravan, a fair gathers at the Gumandev Hanuman temple near Jhagadia (about 20 km from Bharuch), with devotees walking in from Bharuch and Ankleshwar.
A five-day fair at the Shuklatirth temples on the Narmada (about 16-18 km from Bharuch) around Kartik Purnima, drawing thousands of devotees for holy dips and darshan.

At the end of December, the Shree Vishnu Ayyapa Temple on Zadeshwar Road (managed by Bharuch's Kerala community) takes out a festive procession marking the pious Mandalamaasam, with devotees from across the district joining in.
Gujarat's most famous festival: nine nights of garba and dandiya-raas dancing, fasting and late-night celebrations in neighbourhoods and clubs across Anand, Vallabh Vidyanagar and nearby towns.

festival_name: Kali Chaudas Fair, Lambhvel Hanumanji Temple
description: On Kali Chaudas, the day before Diwali, a huge fair is held at the Shree Lambhvel Hanumanji Temple, drawing thousands of devotees from Anand and surrounding villages with great faith and devotion.

Full-moon fairs at Dakor's Ranchhodraiji Temple, about 30 km from Anand. The full moon days of the Kartik, Falgun, Chaitra and Aso months draw an ocean of pilgrims; festivals like Janmashtami, Nanda Mahotsava, Hindola, Rath Yatra, Holi, Dussehra and Annakut are also celebrated with great zeal.
The January kite festival: rooftops across Anand and Charotar fill with kite-flyers from dawn, with traditional undhiyu, jalebi and fafda on the menu.

Gujarat's flagship desert festival held at Dhordo in the White Rann, about 150 km from Mandvi; most travellers combine it with a Mandvi beach-and-heritage leg in the same trip. Folk music, dance, crafts and full-moon desert nights.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya dancing celebrated with great enthusiasm across Kutch, including community garba grounds in Mandvi town.
Gujarat's famous kite festival; Mandvi's beaches and rooftops fill with kite-flyers and the sky over the Gulf of Kutch is crowded with colourful kites.
The Shiva temple at Salaya, after which Kashi Vishvanath Beach is named, sees special night-long prayers and crowds of devotees on Maha Shivratri.

The nine-night festival of the Goddess draws lakhs of devotees to Pavagadh; the temple trust opens the inner sanctum from about 5 AM, with special buses (50+ extra ST buses from Champaner Taleti to Machi), CCTV cover, police and private security. Bhaskar reported over one lakh pilgrims on the 6th-7th days of Aso Navratri, with continuous garba and darshan queues through all nine nights.

The annual fair on the 8th day of the waxing moon in the month of Chaitra at the Kalika Mata Temple, attended by thousands of devotees. Documented in the 19th-century Gazetteers and still held; devotees of Kalika Mata traditionally worship here by beating bell-metal cymbals.
The annual fair on the full-moon day of Chaitra, when large Hindu gatherings come to the summit temple for special poojas, alongside the Dasara (Dussehra) gatherings in autumn.

festival_name: Navratri at Pavagadh Kalika Mata Temple
description: The hilltop Mahakali temple is one of Gujarat's biggest Navratri pilgrimage centres. Large crowds of devotees gather on Pavagadh hill during the nine nights of worship of Goddess Shakti, with the hill illuminated and special rituals held at the shrine.
A traditional fair is held at the Kalika Mata temple on the hill on Chitra sud 8, attended by thousands of devotees, continuing a centuries-old pilgrimage tradition.
Large gatherings of devotees assemble at the Kalika Mata temple at Dasara, alongside the temple's ongoing festival calendar, drawing pilgrims of all communities to the hill.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya raas across Gujarat; Bardoli's temples and public grounds, including Ambika Niketan celebrations, host festive garba gatherings.
Festival of lights celebrated across Bardoli and Gujarat with fireworks, sweets, new clothes and decorated markets.
The kite festival on Makar Sankranti; skies over Gujarat fill with kites and rooftops host kite-flying gatherings with undhiyu and jalebi.
The biggest festival of the year at Dwarkadhish Temple — the birth anniversary of Lord Krishna, celebrated with the midnight Janmotsav (darshan runs past midnight), decorations, and massive crowds.
Diwali at the temple plus the Annakut Mahotsav (Govardhan Puja) — a grand offering of vegetarian food before the deity, celebrated with great pomp at Dwarka's temples.
The festival of colors celebrated with vibrant Holi/Rangotsav darshan at Dwarkadhish Temple and across the city.
The night of Shiva — devotees fast through the day and night, with special pujas and abhishekams at the Nageshwar Jyotirlinga.
Nine nights of Garba and Dandiya Raas celebrated across Dwarka, with temple programs and community dances.
The autumn full-moon festival observed at Dwarkadhish Temple with special prayers and offerings.
The chariot festival — the deities are taken out on decorated chariots through the streets with chanting and singing.
The Kartik full-moon observance, one of the major holy days for darshan at the temple.
The mid-January kite festival; temples in Dwarka hold special observances for the winter-solstice festival.
The biggest festival at Somnath; lakhs of devotees throng the temple for special prayers and rituals through the night, and temple hours and aarti schedules are extended.
The full-moon day of the Kartik month draws large pilgrim crowds for the holy bath at Triveni Sangam and special religious ceremonies at the temple.
The holy month of Shravan brings heightened Shiva worship and heavy pilgrim footfall; the morning aarti shifts earlier and darshan hours are extended.

Gujarat Tourism's annual cultural festival on the white salt desert near Dhordo village (~80 km from Bhuj). Folk music and dance, crafts bazaars, camel rides, and full-moon nights on the salt flats; accommodation at the Rann Utsav Tent City. Permits required for private vehicles at the Dhordo checkpoint.
Nine nights of garba and dandiya-raas dancing celebrated across Gujarat, including Bhuj's public grounds and community mandals; the largest Hindu festival of the region's dance calendar.
Gujarat's international kite festival; the skies over Bhuj and Kutch fill with kites. Travelers are welcome to fly kites from terraces and open grounds.
Night-long Shiva worship; the annual fair at the 10th-century Kera Shiva Temple (22 km south of Bhuj) and observances at Tapkeshwari Temple draw large local crowds.
A uniquely Bhuj celebration: when monsoon rain fills Hamirsar Lake to overflowing ('Augun'), residents gather at the lake for the traditional overflow festivities. Occurs only in good monsoon years.

Celebrated on 31 October at Ekta Nagar to mark Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's birth anniversary, with the PM paying floral tribute at the Statue of Unity. The 2026 edition (150th birth anniversary) features a grand Unity Parade of police, CAPF and NCC contingents, a nationwide Run for Unity, and a fortnight-long cultural festival (31 Oct-15 Nov) with exhibitions of arts, crafts, cuisines and tourism from across India.

Annual festival at Nilkanth Dham, Poicha, held from Bhai Beej to Labh Pancham (in the Kartik month, around Diwali), celebrating the temple with special religious and cultural programmes on its 108-acre campus.

One of Bengaluru's oldest festivals, dedicated to Draupadi, celebrated by the Tigala community with a grand midnight procession from the Dharmaraya Swamy Temple in Thigalarapete. The Karaga bearer balances the sacred pot in a spectacular all-night ritual.

Annual groundnut fair held around the Bull Temple in Basavanagudi, dating to 1537. Farmers offer their first groundnut harvest to Nandi; the temple street fills with groundnut stalls, snacks and nearly a lakh of lamps. Held on the last Monday of Karthika masa.

Widely celebrated across Bengaluru with large public pandals and processions; Ulsoor Lake is a major immersion (visarjan) center. The city's markets and streets take on a festive character for the 10-day festival.

Celebrated with devotion across Bengaluru's temples and neighborhoods; Janapada Loka hosts grand Dasara cultural events. Many Bengalureans also make the day trip to Mysuru for the world-famous Mysuru Dasara procession.

The festival of lights is celebrated citywide with lamps, fireworks and sweets; temples like ISKCON and the Bull Temple area glow through the week. Markets in Chickpet and Malleshwaram bustle with festive shopping.

Karnataka's grandest festival — the 10-day royal Dasara centred on Mysore Palace: the illuminated palace, the Jumbo Savari elephant procession on Vijayadashami, cultural programmes and the Dasara exhibition. The city's peak season.

The chief annual festival of the Cheluvanarayana Swamy Temple at Melukote, when the deity is adorned with the diamond-studded Vairamudi crown and taken out in procession; attended by lakhs of devotees.
The annual float festival at Melukote, when the temple deities are taken on a decorated float across the temple tank (kalyani) — a major draw alongside the Vairamudi celebrations.
The great night of Shiva at Nanjangud's Srikanteshwara Temple (Dakshina Kashi), with special abhishekams through the night and massive pilgrim crowds.
An annual literary festival in Mysuru hosting authors, panel discussions and book events — a growing cultural fixture of the city's December calendar.

Karnataka's state-organized cultural festival recreating the grandeur of the Vijayanagara Empire amid the Hampi ruins - three days of classical and folk music, dance, drama, puppet shows, processions and fireworks around the Virupaksha Temple area.

The annual chariot festival of Virupaksha Temple, when the deity is paraded through Hampi's streets on a grand wooden chariot pulled by devotees, accompanied by music and dance; the temple's biggest religious celebration.

Annual Carnatic music aradhana honouring the saint-composer Purandaradasa, the 'father of Carnatic music', who lived and attained samadhi at Hampi; concerts are held in Hampi and organized by the Purandara Dasara Aradhana Samithi Trust.
Annual celebration of the celestial marriage of Lord Virupaksha and goddess Pampadevi at Virupaksha Temple, marked by special pujas and processions.
The great night of Shiva observed with night-long vigils, special abhisheka of the linga and oil-lamp illuminations at Hampi's principal Shiva temple.

Coorg's most famous festival, distinct from Mysuru's: ten temples of Madikeri (including Durgaparameshwari) parade their deities on grand mantapas in a midnight procession on Vijayadashami night, drawing lakhs of devotees and tourists. The town's peak cultural week.

The holiest day at Talakaveri: at the auspicious moment (tula sankramana) the spring at Brahma Kundike is believed to fill with a gush of water; thousands gather for the teertha snana (holy dip) at the birthplace of the river Kaveri.

The Kodava harvest festival: at midnight, the sheaf of new paddy is cut to the sound of a gunshot, then carried home with a procession; homes feast on thambuttu (mashed banana and sesame) and celebrate for days.

The Kodava festival of weapons: after the transplanting season, families clean and worship their traditional arms (guns, swords, daggers), followed by sporting contests like coconut shooting and feasting on pandi curry.
The biggest festival of the year at Mahabaleshwar Temple; thousands of devotees gather for special pujas and the temple's chariot (ratha) procession honoring Lord Shiva's Atmalinga.
Lord Ganesha's birthday celebrated across the town with special pujas at Maha Ganapati Temple; the deity is traditionally worshipped before darshan at Mahabaleshwar Temple.
The Kartika-month lamp-lighting festival celebrated at Gokarna's temples with rows of oil lamps (deepas); pilgrims bathe at Koti Tirtha and visit Mahabaleshwar Temple.
The festival of lights celebrated town-wide; temples, homes and beachfront establishments are lit with diyas and firecrackers.
The Kannada New Year (Chandramana Ugadi) marked by special temple pujas, mango-leaf decorations and festive meals in homes across the Uttara Kannada coast.

The biennial transfer of Sri Krishna Matha's administration from one of the eight Ashta Mathas to the next, a tradition instituted by Madhvacharya and reformed to a two-year cycle by Vadiraja Tirtha. The handover, held around mid-January, draws lakhs of devotees for the procession, sacred dip and mass annadana.

A seven-day annual festival at Sri Krishna Matha culminating around Makara Sankranti, commemorating the day Madhvacharya installed the Krishna idol in Udupi. All three temple chariots - Brahma Ratha, Garuda Ratha and the small ratha - are drawn in procession on the final day, with the Suvarnotsava closing the celebrations.

The festival of a hundred thousand lamps at Sri Krishna Matha, held after the monsoon when daily utsavas resume (around Uthana Dwadashi). Thousands of oil lamps are lit across the temple precincts and the utsava idols are taken in chariot procession around Car Street.

festival_name: Sri Krishna Janmashtami and Mosaru Kudike
description: Janmashtami is celebrated over three days at the Matha with midnight rituals, the deity dressed as the sporting child, and Gita/Bhagavata chanting. The following afternoon's Mosaru Kudike sees mud pots of turmeric-saffron water hung from poles and broken by costumed revellers as the idol is paraded on Car Street, with tiger-dance troupes and fancy-dress parades.

The annual observance of Madhvacharya's day of departure (Magha Shukla Navami), marked at the Krishna Matha and the Ashta Mathas with special poojas, discourses and feasts honouring the founder of the Dvaita school.

The ritual spirit-worship performances of Tulunadu, held in village shrines across Udupi district in the dry months. Dancers in elaborate costumes embody local guardian spirits to drumming through the night; visitors can sometimes witness performances at rural daivasthanas with local guidance.

A three-day annual Urs (fair) at the Sri Guru Dattatreya Bababudan Swamy Dargah in the Baba Budangiri hills, drawing around 8,000 devotees; both Hindu and Muslim pilgrims attend. The district administration restricts tourist traffic to the hill stations (Mullayanagiri, Bababudangiri, Galikere, Manikyadhara) for the three days, so plan hill visits around it.

Datta Jayanti at the Baba Budangiri Datta Peeta draws large crowds of devotees to the hill shrine in December. Tourist access to the surrounding hill areas may be restricted by the district administration during this period.

The grand 11-day Navaratri festival at the Sringeri Sharadamba Temple, with Shathachandi Homa Poornahuti performed on Mahanavami day. Special pujas, Carnatic music concerts and Vedanta discourses run through the nine nights, and the temple hosts the Vidyarambham ceremony initiating young children into learning on Vijayadashami.

The five-day annual Rathotsava (chariot festival) of the Horanadu Annapoorneshwari Temple, held in the Phalguna month, is the temple's biggest festival and draws heavy crowds. Related celebrations include Navaratri (Sep-Oct) and Deepotsava in the Karthika month.

Akshaya Tritiya (Akshaya Thadige) is celebrated as the birthday of goddess Annapoorneshwari at the Horanadu temple and is considered the temple's main festival; tradition holds that the deity's re-consecration happened on this day. It marks the beginning of Treta Yuga per temple tradition and falls in the Vaishakha month.

Badami's biggest annual event: a month-long religious fair at the Banashankari Devi temple in Cholachagudda, ~5 km from town. Its centerpiece is the Maha Rathotsava, the grand chariot procession of goddess Banashankari held on Paush Purnima, drawing lakhs of devotees from Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The jatre adds cultural programmes, folk theatre (company natakas), a Palya Habba vegetable offering, a boat festival in the temple tank and kilometre-long stalls selling crafts, toys, local food and farm goods.

Annual classical dance festival organised by the Government of Karnataka at the UNESCO-listed Pattadakal temple complex (~22 km from Badami), also called the Chalukya Utsava. A three-day event where renowned artists perform Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, Kathak and other classical forms against the backdrop of the 7th-8th century temples; venues have also included nearby Badami and Aihole.

Mahashivaratri is the main festival at the ancient Mahakuteshwar temple complex in Mahakuta (~13 km from Badami), a Shaiva monastery complex of 6th-7th century Chalukya temples with a natural spring-fed tank (Vishnu Pushkarini). Devotees gather for night-long pujas and a holy dip in the tank; the complex stays open late during the festival.

Annual festival period at Kudala Sangama (~50 km from Badami) observed during the Magha month, along with well-attended Shivaratri celebrations, at the Sangameshwara temple complex where the Krishna and Malaprabha rivers meet. Kudala Sangama is the samadhi place of the 12th-century Lingayat philosopher Basavanna and a major pilgrimage centre; the temple trust provides free food (dasoha) and accommodation during festival periods.
Dasara is celebrated every year in Shivamogga with cultural programmes across the city, marking the victory of good over evil during Navaratri-Vijayadashami.
A major festival at Shivamogga's Shiva temples — notably the Keladi and Ikkeri temples — with night-long worship, abhisheka and large devotee gatherings.
The Marikamba temple festival in Sagara town (about 75 km away), celebrated once every three years with a large temple-car procession, drawing devotees from across the district.
Celebrated with enthusiasm across Shivamogga with Ganesha idols installed in homes and public pandals, prayers, cultural programmes and the final Visarjana procession.
Karnataka's major harvest festival, observed in Shivamogga with kite flying, sesame-jaggery sweets (ellu-bella) and family gatherings.
The major annual festival period at the Sigandur Chowdeshwari Temple, when thousands of devotees gather during Ashada; Navaratri is the other peak pilgrimage period.

Annual car festival of the Chennakeshava Temple, held about 12 days after Ugadi. The Utsava Murti rides a huge wooden chariot for two days (eastern streets on day one, the rest on day two), with a 10-day jatre fair around the temple.
Karnataka tourism's annual cultural festival celebrating Hoysala heritage at Belur and Halebidu, with classical dance and music performances staged near the temples.
Night-long Shiva worship observed with special fervour at the Hoysaleswara Temple in Halebidu; devotees also gather at Belur's temples.
Nine-night festival; notably the famous annual festival of the Lakshmi Devi Temple at Doddagaddavalli, and celebrated across Belur's temples with special pujas.
Festival of lights; the Chennakeshava Temple complex and town are lit with oil lamps and the Deepa Sthambha is illuminated.
Grand anointing of the 57-ft Gommateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola with milk, saffron, sandalwood paste and other offerings; draws lakhs of devotees. Last held in 2018, next expected in 2030.

Fort Kochi's famous year-end carnival (Dec 23/24 - Jan 1): decorated floats, folk performances, beach games, and the midnight burning of the Pappanji effigy on Dec 31 followed by a grand procession on Jan 1.
India's largest international contemporary art biennale, held across Fort Kochi and Mattancherry venues (principal venue Aspinwall House). Biennial; the 6th edition ran Dec 12, 2025 - Mar 31, 2026.
Kerala's harvest festival celebrated across Kochi with Onam sadhya feasts, pookalam flower carpets, boat races and cultural programmes; the Athachamayam procession at Thripunithura marks its start.
Colourful procession at Thripunithura heralding the start of Onam: caparisoned elephants, panchavadyam percussion, folk art forms and floats through the town.

Eight-day annual festival of the Ernakulam Shiva Temple in the Malayalam month of Makaram: kodiyettam flag hoisting, Pakalpooram with caparisoned elephants and panchavadyam, temple arts, and the Arattu holy-bath procession to Durbar Hall Ground.

Ten-day festival at Attukal Bhagavathy Temple culminating in the world's largest annual gathering of women (Guinness record, ~4 million participants in 2026). On the main Pongala day, women cook sweet rice in earthen pots over open hearths across a 7-km radius around the temple as an offering to Attukal Amma. Only women participate; the city is transformed by the ritual.

Kerala's official state festival, a 10-day harvest celebration marking the homecoming of the mythical King Mahabali. In Thiruvananthapuram it is celebrated with pookalam floral carpets, Onasadya vegetarian feasts, cultural performances and temple events; the city hosts government-organised Onam week festivities.

Week-long classical dance festival organised by Kerala Tourism at the Nishagandhi open-air auditorium in Kanakakkunnu Palace grounds, usually in the last week of January. Showcases Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Kathakali and Mohiniyattam by leading exponents; free entry.

Ten-day Carnatic/Hindustani music festival (early January) at Kuthiramalika Palace devoted exclusively to the compositions of Maharaja Swathi Thirunal, organised by Prince Rama Varma and the Travancore Trust. Free, unticketed concerts in the palace courtyard.

Nine-night Navaratri festival at Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple during September-October. Idols of Goddess Saraswati from Padmanabhapuram Palace, the Munnuttinanka idol from Suchindram and Kumaraswamy from Kumarakovil are brought in a ceremonial procession to the Navaratri Mandapam; daily pujas, Saraswati puja and cultural programmes follow.
Kerala's biggest harvest festival, celebrated across Munnar with flower rangolis (pookalam), Onam sadhya feasts and cultural programmes in the tea estates.
Kerala New Year, marked with Vishukkani displays, temple visits and fireworks; celebrated in Munnar's temples and plantation communities.
Women's festival in the Malayalam month of Dhanu with Thiruvathirakali dance performances; observed in Munnar's temples and households.
Widely celebrated in Munnar's tea estates and churches, a legacy of the British planter era, with carols, midnight mass and New Year events in the hill station.
Not a festival but Munnar's signature natural event: the Neelakurinji flower blooms en masse in Eravikulam National Park once every 12 years, carpeting the hills in blue. The last bloom was 2018.
approx_month: Every 12 years (next expected around 2030; bloom window roughly July-October)

description: Kerala's most famous snake boat race, held annually on the second Saturday of August at Punnamada Lake in Alappuzha. Giant chundan vallams (100-120 ft snake boats) with up to 110 oarsmen compete for a silver trophy instituted after Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru's visit in 1952.

One of the oldest snake boat races in Kerala, held on the River Pampa at Champakulam on Moolam day of the Malayalam month Midhunam. It marks the day the Krishna idol was brought by boat for installation at the Ambalappuzha Sree Krishna Temple and opens the boat-race season.

A three-day snake boat race at Payippad Lake, about 35 km from Alappuzha, commemorating the installation of the deity at the Subramanya Swamy Temple, Haripad. Local legend says the idol was found in the Kayamkulam lake after villagers dreamt of it.

The biggest festival of the Mullakkal Rajarajeswari Temple in Alappuzha town, running 41 days from the start of the Malayalam month Vrishchikam to the 11th of Dhanu, with the last 11 days celebrated as Chirappu - marked by caparisoned elephant parades, cultural programmes and a grand final-day annadanam feast.

The 10-day annual festival of the Ambalappuzha Sree Krishna Temple, with caparisoned elephants, panchavadyam percussion ensembles and the ceremonial holy bath (arattu) of the idol in the temple pond, drawing large crowds to the town.

The grand annual feast of St. Sebastian at St. Andrew's Basilica, Arthunkal (also called Makaram Perunnal), lasting about ten days in January. The highlight is the procession of the Milan-made St. Sebastian statue to the beach and back, with devotees crawling on their knees (nercha) to fulfil vows.

Kozhikode District Tourism Promotion Council's flagship cultural festival, held since 1992 across venues including Mananchira Maidan, Kozhikode Beach, Thali Heritage Open Stage and Sarovaram. Four to five days of classical and folk arts, theatre, gazals, rock concerts, martial arts like Kalaripayattu and Theyyam showcases, food stalls serving Malabar cuisine, and amusement rides.

A centuries-old scholarly assembly held at the Tali Maha Shiva Temple, where Vedic scholars gather for debates and recitations. One of Kerala's oldest continuing intellectual traditions, rooted in the Zamorin era.

Annual international crafts fair at the Sargaalaya Kerala Arts & Crafts Village in Iringal, drawing artisans from across India and abroad. Live craft demonstrations, folk performances and stalls selling handmade textiles, woodwork, metal craft and more.

Water-sports and tourism festival at Beypore celebrating the port town's seafaring heritage. Speedboat service connecting Kozhikode Beach to Beypore, parasailing, kayaking demos, cultural programmes and seafood stalls.

The ritual dance-theatre season of North Malabar, when kavus (sacred groves) and ancestral shrines across the Kozhikode–Kannur region host all-night Theyyam performances — elaborate face paint, towering headgear, chenda drumming and trance worship. Performances are religious rituals, not staged shows; go with a local guide and dress modestly.

One of Asia's largest literature festivals, held on Kozhikode Beach each January. Hundreds of authors, poets and thinkers across sessions in English, Malayalam and other Indian languages, plus cultural performances and book stalls.

Kerala's biggest harvest festival, celebrated across Kumily with pookalam (flower carpets), traditional sadhya feasts, folk performances and decorated streets; the town's markets and homestays are at their liveliest.
The Malayalam New Year, marked in Kumily and Peermade with the vishukkani ritual arrangement, temple visits, fireworks and festive meals at the start of the summer season.

The one day each year the ancient Mangaladevi Temple inside Periyar Tiger Reserve opens to devotees - on the Chithra Pournami full moon. Thousands of pilgrims trek or take shared jeeps from Kumily up the forest track for the festival.

The annual Sabarimala pilgrim season; Kumily (~40 km by road from Sabarimala) fills with pilgrims, and the sacred Makarajyothi flame is visible from viewpoints like Parunthumpara and Panchalimedu on Makaravilakku day.
Celebrated at Kumily and Peermade churches with midnight mass, carols and illuminated streets, coinciding with the peak December tourist season in Thekkady.

Kerala's state harvest festival; Thiruvananthapuram hosts the official state Onam week celebrations at Kanakakkunnu grounds with cultural programs, food festivals and the famed Pookalam (flower rangoli) displays.

Mass women's gathering at Attukal Bhagavathy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram (~16 km) — among the world's largest single-day women's congregations. Devotees cook sweet pongala in earthen pots in rows along the streets on the Pooram star of Meenam.

Thiruvananthapuram's 111-day arts festival by the Soorya Stage and Film Society (2024 edition ran Oct 2, 2024–Jan 21, 2025) — the world's longest art festival. Opens with a 10-day dance-and-music festival (Oct 1–10) featuring leading classical dancers and musicians; theatre, film, and Parampara segments follow.
Week-long Carnatic music festival at Kuthiramalika Palace, Thiruvananthapuram (~16 km), celebrating Maharaja Swathi Thirunal's compositions, performed on the palace forecourt.

Week-long classical dance festival (Jan 20–27, per Kerala Tourism convention) at the Nishagandhi open-air auditorium, Kanakakkunnu Palace grounds, Thiruvananthapuram — Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam; free entry.
Nine-night Carnatic music festival at the Navaratri Mandapam in the Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple fort complex, Thiruvananthapuram (~16 km), coinciding with Navaratri/Dussehra.

The 14-day annual festival of the Valliyoorkkavu Bhagavathy Temple near Mananthavady (~24 km from Kalpetta), held in March-April (Malayalam month Meenam) in honour of Goddess Durga's victory over the demon Daruka. Famous for tribal rituals - the Kalamezhuthu ritual on festival nights and folk dances by Wayanad's tribal communities with native percussion on the final day.

A 28-day annual pilgrimage festival at the forest shrine of Akkare Kottiyoor, on the Wayanad-Kannur border. The temporary shrine is built each year in the forest by the Bavali river and dismantled after the festival; rituals like Neyyattam, Ilaneer Veypu and Rohini Aradhana draw lakhs of devotees. (2026 edition ran roughly May 29-June 24.)

Kerala's biggest festival, the 10-day harvest festival honouring King Mahabali, celebrated across Wayanad with Pookalam flower carpets, the Onasadya feast, Vallamkali boat-race telecasts and cultural programmes. Thiruvonam is the main day.
The traditional harvest festival of Wayanad's tribal communities, celebrating the new rice harvest with feasting, folk songs and community rituals in tribal hamlets across the district.

Maha Shivaratri is the biggest annual festival at the Thirunelly Temple (~55 km from Kalpetta), drawing large crowds of pilgrims who bathe in the Papanashini stream and offer ancestral rites (Pithru Tharpanam) at the temple.
The Malayali new year, celebrated across Wayanad with the Vishukkani ritual arrangement, Vishu sadya feast and fireworks; temples and homes mark the start of the new agricultural cycle.

Thrissur Pooram, held at the Thekkinkadu Maidan around Vadakkunnathan Temple, is Kerala's grandest temple festival - the 'mother of all Poorams'. Founded in 1797-98 by Sakthan Thampuran (Raja Rama Varma of Cochin), it brings together ten temples in a friendly rivalry led by Paramekkavu and Thiruvambady. Highlights: caparisoned elephants, the Kudamattam parasol exchange, the Ilanjithara Melam percussion ensemble, and a massive midnight fireworks display. Celebrated on the Pooram asterism in the Malayalam month of Medam.

Pulikali, the tiger dance of Thrissur, is held during the Onam season (fourth day of Onam) on Swaraj Round. Hundreds of performers paint their bodies in vivid tiger stripes and dance to chenda melam rhythms through the streets. Organised by local desams (nine teams in 2026) with Thrissur Corporation support, it is one of Kerala's most photographed folk art spectacles.

Arattupuzha Pooram, at the Arattupuzha Sree Sastha Temple (~15 km from Thrissur), is a 7-day festival in the Malayalam month of Meenam and the oldest pooram tradition in Kerala - the 'mother of all Poorams' that predates Thrissur Pooram. On the final day, 23 deities from neighbouring temples assemble in procession with 60-80 caparisoned elephants and the Sasthavinte Melam of ~200 percussion artists.

The Chembai Sangeetholsavam is a 12-15 day Carnatic music festival held at the Guruvayur Sree Krishna Temple in honour of maestro Chembai Vaidyanatha Bhagavatar, who conducted the festival for nearly 60 years. Now organised by the Guruvayur Devaswom, it draws 2,000-3,000 musicians who perform in an inclusive, non-competitive format, culminating in a group rendition of the Pancharatna Kritis on Guruvayur Ekadasi day (Vrishchikam, mid-November).

Guruvayur Ekadasi is the most important festival of the Guruvayur Sree Krishna Temple, observed on the Ekadasi (11th day) of the bright fortnight in the Malayalam month of Vrishchikam. The temple marks it with Udayasthamana Pooja (dawn-to-dusk worship), Nirmalya Darshan, lamp-lit elephant processions (Vilakku Ekadasi), Dwadasi Panam, and kathakali performances - it commemorates the day Lord Krishna is believed to have revealed the importance of Ekadasi fasting to Arjuna.

Machad Mamangam, also called Machad Kuthira Vela, is a temple festival at Thiruvanikkavu near Wadakkancherry in Thrissur district, organised competitively by five desams (Karumathra, Viruppakka, Mangalam, Parlikadu, Manalithara). Instead of live elephants, it features grand processions of giant wooden horses (kuthira) - a tradition born from a local king's wish to rival the Uthralikkavu Pooram's elephants without real horses. It begins on the first Friday of the Malayalam month of Kumbham with the main vela on the following Tuesday.

Three-day pilgrimage (Dec 30-Jan 1) at Sivagiri Mutt marking the Sree Narayana Guru movement's annual gathering; lakhs of devotees in yellow garb attend discourses, cultural programmes and community feasts. The 93rd pilgrimage was held in 2025-26.
Annual festival of the Janardanaswamy Temple featuring processions and the ritual arattu (holy bath of the deity); the temple's biggest yearly celebration.
Kerala's harvest festival, celebrated across Varkala with floral carpets (pookkalam), feasts (Onam sadya) and cultural performances.
Malayali New Year, marked by the Vishukkani ritual, temple visits and fireworks in Varkala town.
Birth anniversary of Sree Narayana Guru celebrated at Sivagiri Mutt with processions, debates, seminars, cultural shows and community feasts (Samadhi day follows in September).
Amavasya (new-moon) day in the Malayalam month of Karkidakam when thousands perform bali tharpanam (ancestral homage) at Papanasam Beach and the Bali Mandapam in Varkala.

Mumbai's biggest public festival: thousands of community pandals (most famously Lalbaugcha Raja, est. 1934) install Ganesha idols for 10 days of devotion, ending with the grand Anant Chaturdashi immersion processions at Girgaon Chowpatty. In 2026 celebrations ran September 14–25. Expect massive crowds and festive street energy across the city.

Asia's largest free multidisciplinary street arts festival, held annually in the Kala Ghoda precinct of South Mumbai since 1999. Nine days of art installations, music, dance, theatre, literature, heritage walks, and food stalls across venues like Cross Maidan, CSMVS, and Jehangir Art Gallery. The 2026 edition ran January 31–February 8; the festival always opens on the first Saturday of February.

festival_name: Bandra Fair (Feast of Our Lady of the Mount)
description: The week-long fair around the Feast of the Nativity of Mary at the Basilica of Our Lady of the Mount in Bandra. A ~300-year-old tradition mixing pilgrimage with a carnival: ~150 church stalls and 400+ BMC stalls selling food, sweets (like kadio bodio), religious articles, and games. In 2026 the fair ran September 13–20, starting on the Sunday after the September 8 feast day.

The Marathi New Year, celebrated on Chaitra Shukla Pratipada across Maharashtra. Mumbai homes hoist a 'gudi' (decorated bamboo flag) and the day is marked with festive meals of puran poli and shrikhand, rangoli, and new-venture rituals. Processions and cultural events happen across the city.

Nagpur's unique centuries-old festival held in the month of Bhadrapada (Aug-Sep). Giant effigies called Marbats — symbolizing evil forces, social evils and issues troubling society — are paraded through the city with music and chants alongside smaller Badgya effigies, and then set ablaze, symbolizing the triumph of good over evil. It blends cultural tradition with sharp social commentary.

Observed on 14-15 October at Deekshabhoomi, commemorating Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's mass conversion to Buddhism with lakhs of followers on 14 October 1956. Lakhs of Buddhists gather annually (coinciding with Dussehra/Ashoka Vijayadashami); mass conversions continue at the site.

Grand annual procession on Ram Navami (Chaitra, March-April) starting from Shri Poddareshwar Ram Mandir in Mahal, Nagpur, and passing through Itwari, Mahal, Sitabuldi and Variety Square. Features 90+ jhankis (tableaus) of Ramayana scenes, the Ram Rath, dhol-tasha and lezim performances. A 60+ year tradition (the 60th yatra was held in 2026, attended by the CM and Nitin Gadkari).

Organised by MTDC since 1996 at Nagardhan (Nandiwardhan) Fort in Ramtek, honouring the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa — who composed the Meghaduta at Ramtek. A multi-day festival of classical music, dance and drama with national artists, held to promote tourism in the region.

One of the four Simhastha Kumbh sites; millions bathe in the Godavari at Ramkund (Nashik) and at Trimbakeshwar. The next cycle's ceremony period was announced by the Maharashtra government as 31 Oct 2026-24 Jul 2028, with the main Amrit Snan bathing days in August-September 2027.

Annual vineyard music festival at Sula Vineyards, Nashik, mixing Indian and international artists, wine, food and camping. The 14th edition was held 1-2 Feb 2025 (after a 5-year break); the 15th edition was held 31 Jan-1 Feb 2026 and sold out.
Annual 2-day festival organized by Maharashtra Tourism, listed on the Ministry of Tourism's utsav.gov.in portal: around 50 grape farmers and ~12 wineries showcase the region's wine and grape culture.
The biggest festival at Saptashrungi Devi Temple, Vani (Nashik district), observed from Rama Navami to Chaitra Poornima; up to ~1 million devotees attend over the festival days.
Five-day winter classical dance and music festival held in Aurangabad, organized with the Aurangabad Festival Committee and MTDC; accompanied by a Kalagram crafts haat and handicrafts fair.
MTDC's classical dance and music festival staged at/around Ellora and Soneri Mahal, showcasing Indian classical arts with regional artisan stalls.
approx_month: December (winter; timing has varied by edition)

description: Annual international film festival held in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar since 2014; editions typically run January 11-15.

festival_name: Hanuman Jayanti at Bhadra Maruti Temple
description: The year's biggest gathering at the Bhadra Maruti Temple in Khuldabad — one of only three temples in India with Hanuman in a reclining posture — drawing huge pilgrim crowds for special prayers and aartis.
The principal annual festival at the Grishneshwar Jyotirlinga near Ellora: abhishekam, devotional singing and all-night vigils drawing thousands of devotees.

festival_name: Upvan Sanskruti Arts Festival (Vihang Sanskruti Arts Festival)

description: Sharadiya Navratri is the grandest festival at the Ambabai temple - nine nights of special alankars (decorations), music and massive pilgrim crowds. During Navratri, the goddess's palanquin procession travels from the Mahalakshmi Temple to the Temblai Temple, her 'sister' shrine on Temblai Hill.

Twice a year - around January 31-February 2 and November 9-11 - the setting sun's rays pass through the Mahadwar and fall directly on the Mahalakshmi idol for three evenings. This celebrated solar-architectural event, noted by the Devasthan committee, draws thousands of devotees to the temple.

The annual fair on the full moon of Chaitra (and Vaishakha) at the Jyotiba Temple, Wadi Ratnagiri. Lakhs of devotees gather as the hill turns pink with thrown gulaal; highlights include the Sasan Kathi (tall bamboo-pole) procession and the evening palanquin procession of Lord Jyotiba to Goddess Yamai's temple with fireworks.

An annual multi-day international film festival celebrating Kolhapur's rich cinema heritage, honoring filmmakers with the Kalamaharshi Baburao Painter Award (the 7th edition ran in February 2019 with Hungarian cinema as the focus country). Recent editions could not be verified - confirm the current year's schedule before planning around it.

Solapur's biggest annual religious fair, held at the Shri Siddheshwar Temple. The 900-year-old Gadda Yatra centers on a symbolic marriage ritual of Lord Siddheshwar — two Nandi Dhwaja poles (bride and groom) are carried in procession, with the 'marriage' performed on Makar Sankranti day — followed by a 15-day cultural fair around the temple lake.

One of Maharashtra's largest pilgrimages: lakhs of warkaris walk from Alandi and Dehu to Pandharpur in Solapur district, converging on the Vitthal Rukmini Temple for Ashadhi Ekadashi. Pandharpur is ~70 km from Solapur city and the Wari routes pass through Solapur district.

The second great yatra to Pandharpur, when warkaris again gather at the Vitthal Rukmini Temple on Kartiki Ekadashi. A major pilgrimage event in the Solapur region with special rituals at the temple and on the Chandrabhaga ghats.

festival_name: Sharadiya Navratri at Tulja Bhavani, Tuljapur
description: The nine-night Sharadiya Navratri festival at the Shri Tulja Bhavani Temple in Tuljapur (~45 km from Solapur), one of Maharashtra's 3.5 Shakti Peethas. The temple's own site describes it as the most important worship period of the goddess, drawing lakhs of devotees; a Shakambari Navratri is also celebrated in December-January.

The biggest religious fair of Amravati, held over the nine days of Navratri (Ashwin, before Dussehra) at the ancient Ambadevi Temple. The temple authorities and people celebrate with cultural and religious programs, special pujas, and a huge mela that draws visitors from all walks of life across Vidarbha. Devotees also visit the adjacent Ekvira Devi Temple during the festival.

Annual pilgrimage held on Kartik Purnima to the Vitthal Rukmini Temple atop the hill at Kaundanyapur, about 45 km from Amravati, believed to be Rukmini's maternal home. Thousands of devotees from the Vidarbha region walk in groups wearing traditional Marathi caps, chanting abhangs, with women performing the fugdi dance; the yatra runs for two days.

Annual three-day yatra at the samadhi of Rashtra Sant Tukdoji Maharaj at Mozari (Tiosa) on NH-6, held around Ashwin Vadya 5. Historical fair records note attendance of around 75,000 devotees over the period, making it one of the major religious gatherings of Amravati district.

A major Navratra festival celebrated from the 1st to the 9th of Ashwin Shukla at Ner Pinglai in Morshi taluka of Amravati district, recorded in Amravati's historical fair listings with attendance of around 50,000. It is one of the district's prominent Devi festivals alongside the Ambadevi Navratri.

One of the three principal festivals of the Shri Saibaba Sansthan Trust, celebrating the birth of Lord Rama. Shirdi holds special processions, kirtans, and programmes across the temple complex, drawing large crowds.

The full-moon day honouring the guru (spiritual teacher), among the biggest observances at the Samadhi Mandir. Devotees gather in large numbers for special aartis and darshan; listed among the trust's three main festivals on sai.org.in and Wikipedia's Shirdi temple infobox.

The biggest annual festival in Shirdi, marking the Mahasamadhi (passing) of Sai Baba in October 1918. The trust organises a multi-day Punyatithi Utsav with processions, cultural programmes, and special aartis; lakhs of devotees attend.

festival_name: Navratri at Ekvira Devi Temple, Karla
description: The 9-day Ashwin Navratri (Shukla Paksha Pratipada to Navami) at the Ekvira Devi Temple beside the Karla Caves is Lonavala's biggest religious gathering: thousands of Koli and Agri devotees climb the hill with folk dances, music and illumination, and the goddess is taken out in the Ekvira Devi Palki procession on the ninth day (Ashtami and Navami are the most important dates). In 2026 the festival ran October 11-20 with the palki on October 19/20.

festival_name: Chaitra Navratra at Ekvira Devi Temple, Karla
description: The spring Navratra fair at the Ekvira Devi Temple near the Karla Caves — the second peak pilgrimage season after Ashwin Navratri, when Koli folk celebrations and special pujas fill the temple complex.

festival_name: Ganesh Chaturthi, Janmashtami and Diwali at Narayani Dham
description: The white-marble Narayani Dham Temple in Lonavala celebrates Ganesh Chaturthi, Janmashtami and Diwali with special enthusiasm, drawing large devotional crowds to its 5-acre complex.

Yearly festival marking the start of summer, supported by the All India Strawberry Growers Association. Stalls with strawberry-based edibles, folk dance performances, orchestra, watercolour tattoos, mehndi stalls, and strawberry-picking strolls. Thousands attend each year.
The main festival of the Mahabaleshwar Temple, drawing large crowds for the Shivratri celebrations at the town's principal shrine.

The 10-day Ganeshotsav is celebrated across Alibaug very traditionally — families install Ganpati idols at home and neighbourhoods set up large community idols with processions, music, fireworks and modaks through the ten days.
The rural Bail Pola festival honours bullocks and oxen: farmers bathe, massage, paint and garland their bulls and worship them, with local competitions and events in Alibaug's farming villages.

An annual beachside festival with sand art competitions, boat races, traditional dance and music performances, and food stalls serving local coastal cuisine — organised by local camps and groups, also around Holi and New Year.
An annual winter festival celebrating local culture with music, dance and handicrafts, giving visitors a taste of the hill station's traditions.
Matheran's biggest religious festival, celebrated with great pomp across the town for about ten days in September, reflecting the hill station's communal harmony.
An annual trail-running event held in/around Matheran with 5 km, 10 km, 25 km and 50 km editions (summer edition listed on MeraEvents), popular with endurance runners across Maharashtra.

Ganesh Chaturthi is the biggest festival at the Swayambhu Ganpati Temple in Ganpatipule, drawing lakhs of devotees to Ratnagiri district. The temple holds special pujas and celebrations through the 10-day festival, and the town's beaches and markets come alive with pilgrims.

festival_name: Maghi Ganesh Jayanti (Ganesh Jayanti) at Ganpatipule
description: Ganesh Jayanti (Magh Shukla Chaturthi), celebrating Lord Ganesha's birth, is the second major festival at the Ganpatipule temple, attracting thousands of devotees for special darshan, aartis and the hill pradakshina.

The Koli fishing community of the Konkan coast, including Ratnagiri's Mandvi, Bhatye and Mirya beaches, celebrates Narali Pournima on the Shravana full moon by offering coconuts to the sea god Varuna. Decorated boats, Koli dances and feasts mark the end of the monsoon fishing ban and the reopening of the fishing season.

The coconut festival celebrated on the full-moon day of the Hindu month of Shravana (July-August) by Maharashtra's Koli fishing communities, including Malvan's fisherfolk. Coconuts are offered to the sea god Varuna with decorated boats, music and dance, marking the end of the monsoon and the safe reopening of the fishing season. Raksha Bandhan falls on the same day.

An 800-year-old folk-theatre art form popular in Sindhudurg and North Goa, especially in and around Malvan, depicting the ten incarnations of Lord Vishnu. Performed by local farmer-artists through the night, mainly during the village 'Saptah' (the grand annual worship of the village deity), when villagers also sell homemade khaja, kadak ladoo and pickles. The main parvani (event) of Malvan's villages.

Annual pre-monsoon firefly season when thousands of fireflies light up the forests around Bhandardara, Arthur Lake and Samrad village. Local camping operators run overnight firefly-camping trips with guided night forest walks, bonfire and meals; peak sightings are the last week of May through the first week of June, roughly mid-May to mid-June.
Annual Mahashivratri celebration at the 9th-century Amruteshwar Shiva Temple in Ratanwadi, drawing devotees for prayers and rituals at the ancient Hemadpanthi shrine.

During Navratri, devotees from nearby villages trek up Kalsubai to the summit temple of Goddess Kalsubai as a religious pilgrimage, making the mountain a major festive gathering point in the Bhandardara region.

An annual seasonal nature event in the forests around Igatpuri and Kasara, when lakhs of fireflies light up the pre-monsoon forest. Peak sightings are mid-May to mid-June (roughly May 17 - June 22); campsites around Igatpuri host overnight firefly camping experiences on no-moon nights.

One of the four Kumbh Melas, held every 12 years in Nashik district with ritual bathing at Ramkund in Nashik and the Trimbakeshwar Shiva temple on the Godavari. The next edition runs July 17 - August 17, 2027; the Igatpuri-Nashik road is being widened for the expected pilgrim influx.

A real annual festival of Indian classical dance and music organised by the Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation (MTDC) together with the Aurangabad Festival Committee, spotlighting the Ajanta and Ellora cave heritage. Originally staged against the Kailasa backdrop; recent editions have been held at Soneri Mahal in Aurangabad. Reported in The Hindu BusinessLine (2012 return after a 3-year gap) and recent quiz/heritage references.

Major annual festival at the Grishneshwar Jyotirlinga Temple - special abhishekam rituals, hymns and all-night vigils draw large pilgrim crowds. Shravan month (July-August) also sees very large assemblies and extended temple hours.

Tamil Nadu's biggest harvest festival, celebrated over four days (Bhogi, Thai Pongal, Mattu Pongal, Kaanum Pongal). Families cook the sweet pongal dish in new pots at sunrise, decorate homes with kolam, and honour cattle; Jallikattu bull-taming events happen in southern districts.

One of the world's largest classical music festivals, held across hundreds of sabhas in Chennai during the Tamil month of Margazhi. Carnatic music concerts and Bharatanatyam dance performances run from morning to night, drawing artists and rasikas from around the globe.

The festival of lights, celebrated with oil lamps, fireworks, new clothes and sweets. In Tamil Nadu it is traditionally observed a day earlier than in much of North India, and Chennai's markets and temples are at their liveliest.

A city heritage celebration around Madras Day (22 August), marking the founding of the city in 1639. It features heritage walks, talks, exhibitions and food trails organised by citizen groups across Chennai.

The grandest day of the 10-day Panguni Peruvizha at Mylapore's Kapaleeshwarar Temple, when the idols of Lord Kapaleeshwarar, Goddess Karpagambal and the 63 Nayanmar saints are taken in a massive street procession drawing lakhs of devotees.

Madurai's grand month-long festival at the Meenakshi Amman Temple: the coronation of Goddess Meenakshi, her celestial wedding (Thirukalyanam) with Sundareswarar, the car procession, and the climax - Lord Kallazhagar entering the Vaigai river. Attracts millions of devotees.
The float festival at Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam: the deities of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar are taken around the great temple tank on a decorated illuminated float.
The famous bull-taming sport held at Alanganallur near Madurai during the Pongal season - one of Tamil Nadu's best-known traditional spectacles.
Nine nights of goddess worship, celebrated grandly at the Meenakshi Amman Temple with Golu doll displays - a nod to Vilacheri's doll-making tradition.
Annual temple festival at the Meenakshi Amman Temple during the Tamil month of Avani.
The festival of lights, celebrated across Madurai's temples with rows of oil lamps - especially atmospheric at the hill temples.
The biggest festival at the Marudhamalai Murugan temple, drawing huge crowds of devotees to the hill shrine for kavadi processions and special pujas during the Tamil month of Thai.

Coimbatore's guardian-deity car festival in the Tamil month of Maasi, when the temple chariot rolls through Raja Street, Oppanakara Street, Vysial Street and Big Bazaar Street amid city-wide celebrations.

The famous fire-walking (Kundam) festival at the Bannari Mariamman Temple near Sathyamangalam (~65 km), held in the Tamil month of Panguni; lakhs of devotees attend and Erode district observes a local holiday.
The principal annual festival at the Perur Pateeswarar temple, celebrating the celestial wedding of Shiva and Parvati with processions and special abhishekams.
Monsoon water festival honouring the Noyyal river, observed on the riverbank near Perur with offerings of lamps and flowers as the river swells with the season's rains.
The festival of lamps, when rows of oil lamps are lit at Marudhamalai and temples across Coimbatore on the Karthigai full moon, mirroring the celebrations at Tiruvannamalai.

The most important festival at the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple in Srirangam, celebrated over 21 days in the Tamil month of Margazhi. Lakhs of devotees throng the temple to pass through the Paramapada Vasal (Gate of Paradise), which is opened for this occasion. It is one of the largest Vaishnavite festivals in South India.

The float festival at the Mariamman Teppakulam in Tiruchirappalli, when the temple deity is taken on a decorated raft around the illuminated tank. Sources conflict on the exact timing (January-February vs the Tamil month of Panguni, March-April) - treat the window as approximate.

The Chithirai Brahmotsavam at the Samayapuram Mariamman Temple is one of the temple's biggest annual festivals, drawing lakhs of pilgrims. The Poochoriyal flower festival in the Tamil month of Masi (February-March) precedes it, when devotees shower the goddess with flowers.

The 11-day Thai Poosam festival, celebrated at Murugan temples including Viralimalai and at Samayapuram, when devotees carry kavadi offerings in fulfilment of vows. Temple streets fill with processions and folk performances.

The annual Brahmotsavam at the Jambukeswarar Temple in Thiruvanaikaval during the Tamil month of Panguni, featuring a grand temple car (ther) procession around the Mada streets of this Pancha Bhoota Sthala.

The monsoon festival honouring the Cauvery river, celebrated on the 18th of the Tamil month of Aadi when the river traditionally swells with fresh water. Devotees gather at the Amma Mandapam ghat in Srirangam to offer flowers, lamps and sweet rice to the river.

The full-moon festival at the Kumari Amman Temple, drawing lakhs of devotees to Kanyakumari. Special pujas are held through the night and pilgrims take a holy dip at the Triveni Sangam where the three seas meet.
Nine nights of grand celebrations honouring the goddess at the Kumari Amman Temple and the Suchindram Temple, with special alankarams, music, and processions on the final days.
Kanyakumari's three-day tourism cultural festival featuring music, dance and arts performances, organised to showcase the district's culture to visitors.
The new-moon day in the Tamil month of Aadi, when thousands gather at the Triveni Sangam for a holy dip and to perform ancestor rites (tarpanam) for the departed.
The four-day Tamil harvest festival (Bhogi, Thai Pongal, Mattu Pongal, Kaanum Pongal) celebrated widely across Kanyakumari district with sweet pongal cooking, cattle honours and family gatherings.
The annual car festival (therottam) at the Suchindram Thanumalayan Temple in the Tamil month of Masi, when the temple deities are taken out in a grand chariot procession.
The biggest festival at the Ramanathaswamy Temple, celebrated over 10 days with the temple filled with Shiva devotees; special abhishekams and night-long worship mark the occasion.
The divine marriage of Lord Ramanathaswamy and Goddess Vishalakshi (Parvathy), celebrated as an auspicious occasion with large devotee participation at the temple.
Nine-night festival honouring the Goddess at the Ramanathaswamy Temple, one of its major annual celebrations.
The spring festival of the Ramanathaswamy Temple, celebrated with processions and special rituals.
On this new-moon day in the Tamil month of Aadi, thousands of pilgrims gather at Agni Theertham to offer prayers and rites to departed ancestors.
Annual coronation festival at the Kothandaramaswamy Temple near Dhanushkodi in the Tamil month of Aani, commemorating Rama crowning Vibhishana as king of Lanka.

Annual Carnatic music festival at Thiruvaiyaru (~13 km from Thanjavur) honouring saint-composer Thyagaraja at his samadhi; the 176th aradhana's Pancharatna rendition fell on 2023-01-11. Musicians from across the world perform the Pancharatna kritis in unison - the biggest classical music gathering in the region.

Birth anniversary celebrations of Rajaraja Chola I at the Brihadisvara Temple, observed with special pujas and cultural programmes; the 1041st Sathaya Vizha fell around 2026-10-22 per published reports.
The great night of Shiva, observed with night-long vigils and special abhishekams at the Brihadisvara Temple and Shiva temples across Thanjavur district.
Tamil Nadu's harvest festival in mid-January (Thai month), celebrated across Thanjavur with the ritual boiling of rice, tributes to the sun and cattle, and family feasts.
Nine-night festival honouring the goddess, celebrated at Amman temples including Punnainallur Mariamman with special alankarams, kolu displays in homes and cultural programmes.
Annual 10-day show; 128th edition held May 18-28, 2026 (devdiscourse). Held at Government Botanical Garden.
State-run annual summer season festival; boat races at Ooty Lake. Held at Ooty (boat races at Ooty Lake, cultural events).
21st edition held May 14-18, 2026 (devdiscourse). Held at Government Rose Garden.
Annual fruit show at Sim's Park, Coonoor.
Annual January festival celebrating Nilgiri tea; dates vary by year. Held at Ooty.
Main annual festival of the Elk Hill Murugan Temple; falls late Jan-early Feb (MakeMyTrip).

Kodaikanal's biggest annual celebration, a 10-day festival organised by the Tamil Nadu Tourism Department at Bryant Park. It features the famous flower show, boat races on Kodaikanal Lake, fruit shows, cultural programs with Bharatanatyam, Oyilattam and Mayilattam dances, food and craft stalls, and adventure sports.

The centrepiece of the summer festival, organised by the Department of Horticulture at Bryant Park. It showcases floral sculptures and topiary shaped like animals and famous figures, vegetable creations, and blooms brought from neighbouring villages competing for prizes.

The four-day Tamil harvest festival (Bhogi, Surya Pongal, Mattu Pongal, Kanum Pongal) celebrated across Kodaikanal, dedicated to the Sun God Surya. Households cook the ritual pongal dish of rice, milk and jaggery, and cattle are decorated and honoured on Mattu Pongal.
A winter festival in Kodaikanal where visitors sample many varieties of tea and enjoy authentic South Indian delicacies, celebrating the hill station's tea culture and tourism.

The rare Neelakurinji flower blooms only once every 12 years and carpets the Palani Hills around Kodaikanal in blue and purple. The bloom season draws botanists, nature lovers and tourists from across the world for a once-in-a-generation spectacle.

Annual 30-day classical dance festival organised by the Tamil Nadu Tourism Department, held on an open-air stage against the Shore Temple and Arjuna's Penance backdrop. Features Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, Kathakali, Mohiniyattam, Odissi and Kathak exponents plus folk dancers, typically on weekends from late December into January.

Tamil Nadu's harvest festival, celebrated in mid-January (Thai month) with the ritual boiling of rice with jaggery and milk, tributes to the sun and cattle, and family feasts. Tourist offices organise celebrations for visitors; it overlaps with the dance festival season in Mahabalipuram.

Tamil festival on the Magam nakshatra of the Masi month. At Mahabalipuram it has two faces: the Thirukadalmallai (Sthalasayana Perumal) temple takes the deities in grand procession to the beach for a ceremonial sea bath, and thousands of Irular tribal families gather on the shore for a week of rituals, music and dance by the sea.

The principal annual brahmotsavam of the Sthalasayana Perumal (Thirukadalmallai) Temple, held in the Tamil month of Chithirai, with processions, special pujas and decorated deity parades through the town.
The Tamil New Year in mid-April, observed across Tamil Nadu including Mahabalipuram with temple visits, festive meals and family gatherings marking the start of the Chithirai month.

The flagship annual cultural festival of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, organised by the A&N Administration in Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair), featuring folk dances, music performances, food stalls, handicraft exhibitions and water-sports events.
Annual week-long fair held at Swaraj Dweep (Havelock), commemorating Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's association with the islands; includes cultural programmes, exhibitions and local food stalls.
Annual festival centred on the beaches of Sri Vijaya Puram such as Corbyn's Cove, with beach sports, cultural shows, sand-sculpture and entertainment programmes organised by the tourism department.
Annual music festival held in Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair) during the monsoon season, featuring local and mainland artists performing across genres.
The A&N Tourism Department organises events and special programmes across Sri Vijaya Puram and the islands to mark World Tourism Day, including cultural shows and guided heritage walks.

The Andaman & Nicobar Islands' flagship annual festival, organized by the UT administration, usually held in early-to-mid January over ~5-10 days at the ITF Ground, Port Blair.
